clinicalPearls: Sinus node dysfunction (SND), also termed sick sinus syndrome, typically presents with fatigue, exercise intolerance, dyspnea, or syncope from a slow rate or pauses; the key diagnostic step is correlating symptoms with bradycardia/pauses on ECG or ambulatory monitoring (p.1917-1918).

Tachycardia-bradycardia (tachy-brady) syndrome is a subset of SND: high rates (most commonly atrial fibrillation) alternating with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses after the tachycardia terminates; the drugs needed for rate control often worsen the bradycardia, frequently prompting pacemaker implantation (p.1919).

AV block is classified on ECG: first-degree = fixed PR prolongation >200 ms with all impulses conducted; second-degree = intermittent failure of conduction (Mobitz I/Wenckebach with progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat vs Mobitz II with fixed PR before a dropped beat); third-degree = complete AV dissociation with ventricular rate slower than atrial rate (p.1925-1926).

Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block typically involves the AV node, is hemodynamically stable, and in the absence of symptoms does NOT usually warrant pacing; Mobitz II is usually infranodal, associated with QRS widening and a less reliable escape rhythm, carries a risk of sudden death, and requires permanent pacing even when asymptomatic (p.1925).

Escape morphology localizes block: a narrow QRS escape implies AV-nodal/proximal-His block with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape implies distal His or bundle-branch block with a slower, less reliable rhythm (p.1926).

AV block from acute MI is more common with inferior MI but is usually proximal (AV node), with a stable narrow escape >40/min and often reversible; AV block in anterior MI is usually distal/infranodal, gives wide unstable escape rhythms, and carries a worse prognosis with high mortality (p.1926-1927).

Lyme carditis is a classic reversible infectious cause of AV block (usually nodal, narrow junctional escape >40/min) that typically resolves within about a week of antibiotic therapy; AV block with infective endocarditis should raise concern for a perivalvular abscess requiring urgent surgical consultation (p.1927).

AV block that develops at a younger age (≤60 years) warrants advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, or FDG-PET) to evaluate for infiltrative disease such as sarcoidosis, since age-related progressive conduction-system fibrosis is otherwise the most common cause (p.1928).

Permanent pacing is the only reliable long-term therapy for symptomatic irreversible bradycardia; there is NO established heart-rate threshold below which pacing is automatically indicated, and the decision is driven by symptom-bradycardia correlation (p.1917, p.1922).

Initial management of any bradyarrhythmia is to identify and eliminate reversible causes and assess the safety/reliability of the escape rhythm before deciding on temporary or permanent pacing (p.1922, p.1929).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bradyarrhythmias arise from abnormalities of the specialized conduction tissues. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker (resting rate 60-100/min); its pacemaker cells have no true resting potential and depolarize spontaneously in phase 4 driven by the funny current (If) plus T- and L-type calcium currents, with calcium (not sodium) carrying the slow phase-0 upstroke. SA node function is dominated by parasympathetic tone at baseline (intrinsic heart rate ~100-110/min after autonomic blockade); intrinsic rate declines ~5-6 beats/min per decade of age. SA node dysfunction reflects problems of impulse formation (sinus arrest) or impulse conduction (sinoatrial exit block), and is most often due to age-related fibrosis and loss of pacemaker myocytes. In the AV node, conduction is decremental and depends on L-type calcium current; the node and proximal His are richly innervated by autonomic input, whereas the His bundle and distal conduction system are NOT influenced by autonomic tone. Acquired AV conduction disease is most commonly due to fibrosis/sclerosis/calcification of the conduction system (~50% of cases: senile degeneration/Lev's disease, Lenegre's disease, aortic-annular calcification). Block is anatomically nodal (vagally modulated, stable narrow escape) or infranodal (His-Purkinje, unstable wide escape, higher risk).
additionalDifferentials: Sinus arrest vs sinoatrial exit block (type I fixed delay; type II Mobitz I progressive vs Mobitz II fixed pattern)
Tachy-brady (sick sinus) syndrome with post-conversion offset pauses
Chronotropic incompetence (failure to raise rate with demand; can be missed on standard exercise testing)
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity and cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope
Physiologic/athletic sinus bradycardia and sleep-related vagal pauses
First- vs second-degree (Mobitz I vs II) vs third-degree (complete) AV block
AV-nodal vs infranodal (His-Purkinje) level of block; bifascicular/trifascicular block
Congenital AV block (maternal SLE, congenital heart defects)
infectionMimics: Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi) causing AV block
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug/medication effect (beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone and other antiarrhythmics, clonidine, lithium, etc.)
Increased vagal tone (sleep, well-conditioned athlete, cough/micturition/vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity)
Sleep apnea (high vagal tone during apneic events)
Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre, Lamin A/C cardiomyopathy)
Iatrogenic: cardiac/valve surgery, TAVR, alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation injury, spinal cord injury, post heart transplant
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG (cornerstone; capture rhythm and assess QRS width of escape)
Ambulatory/longer-term monitoring (Holter, mobile cardiac telemetry, event/implantable loop recorders, wearable ECG watches) to obtain symptom-rhythm correlation
Exercise/treadmill testing to assess maximum heart rate and chronotropic competence
Transthoracic echocardiography for structural heart disease
Advanced cardiac imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, FDG-PET, Tc-PYP) when infiltrative disease suspected or AV block at ≤60 years
Vagal maneuvers / carotid sinus massage and atropine/isoproterenol challenge to localize level of block

Invasive electrophysiology study with His-bundle electrogram (AH interval for AV node <130 ms; HV interval for His-Purkinje ≤55 ms) reserved for selected/uncertain cases; SNRT/SACT rarely used and NOT an absolute pacing indication
redFlags: Syncope or presyncope (Stokes-Adams attack) with documented bradyarrhythmia
Mobitz type II second-degree AV block (risk of sudden death; infranodal; pace even if asymptomatic)
High-grade or third-degree (complete) AV block, especially with a wide-complex/slow escape rhythm
Wide-complex escape rhythm at ~30/min (implies low/unreliable block) vs benign narrow junctional escape ~45/min
AV block with anterior MI (extensive infarction, distal block, high mortality)
AV block with infective endocarditis (suggests perivalvular abscess; urgent surgical consult)
HV interval >100 ms in bundle branch block (~10% annual incidence of complete block; indicates need for pacing)
harrison.prognosis: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia has NOT been associated with adverse outcomes and generally does not warrant pacing; symptomatic SND is benign in terms of mortality and is treated to relieve symptoms. AV block prognosis depends critically on the level of block: AV-nodal (Mobitz I) block tends to be stable with a reliable junctional escape and good prognosis, whereas infranodal block (Mobitz II, distal third-degree) has unreliable escape rhythms and risk of sudden death. AV block complicating anterior MI carries high mortality, while inferior-MI nodal block is often transient and reversible. With appropriate permanent pacing, symptomatic bradyarrhythmias have an excellent prognosis. An HV interval >100 ms predicts ~10% annual progression to complete block.
pitfalls: Treating asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or sleep/athletic vagal pauses with a pacemaker - these generally are NOT pacing indications; always check whether pauses occurred during sleep.
Missing reversible causes (drugs, hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia/electrolytes, ischemia, sleep apnea, increased vagal tone, hypothermia, raised ICP) before committing to permanent pacing.
Overlooking Lyme carditis as a reversible cause of AV block (typically resolves within ~1 week of antibiotics) - a treatable cause that should not lead to an unnecessary permanent pacemaker.
Failing to suspect a perivalvular abscess when AV block develops during infective endocarditis.
Treating Mobitz II or high-grade/complete infranodal block as benign - it requires pacing even without symptoms, unlike Mobitz I.
In 2:1 AV block, ECG cannot reliably distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II; clues (PR <160 ms with wide QRS suggesting infranodal) or EP study may be needed.
Missing chronotropic incompetence because a patient achieves a normal maximum heart rate on standard exercise testing despite inadequate rate during daily activity.
Misjudging a normal heart-transplant resting rate (~90-110/min due to denervation) as normal when it may represent chronotropic incompetence.
harrison.severityClassification: ECG-based AV block grading: First-degree (PR >200 ms, all impulses conducted, usually AV-nodal delay) -> Second-degree (intermittent failure; Mobitz I/Wenckebach = progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat, usually nodal/stable; Mobitz II = fixed PR before dropped beat, usually infranodal/wide QRS/unstable) -> Third-degree/complete (complete AV dissociation, ventricular rate slower than atrial). SND subtypes: sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block (type I, type II Mobitz I/II), tachy-brady syndrome, chronotropic incompetence. Pacing-indication classes (ACC/AHA/HRS): Class I (complete/high-grade or acquired Mobitz II block when irreversible - pace regardless of symptoms; symptomatic irreversible 2nd/3rd-degree block), Class IIa/IIb (symptom- or disease-dependent for milder block), Class III: Harm (asymptomatic physiologic bradycardia/pauses).
